extractions.quote: A 58 year-old woman presented with a clinical picture of progressive quadriparesis, sensory loss, sphincter dysfunction, painful muscle spasms in the upper and lower limbs and continuous muscle unit activity in electromyography. She developed hepatitis, pancreatitis and HCVRNA was detected in the plasma by reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). Postmortem histopathological examination showed encephalomyelitis with perivascular lymphocyte cuffing, infiltration and neuronal loss mainly affecting the brainstem and cervical spinal cord. The RT-PCR analysis of the postmortem brain, brainstem, liver, pancreas, plasma and CSF samples revealed the presence of HCV genome in all specimens except CSF. Clinical features, postmortem histopathology and PCR results and the possible etiopathogenesis of PEWR are briefly discussed.

extractions.quote: Postmortem examination (OT-30-92) showed encephalo myelitis of the brain, brainstem and spinal cord affecting both gray and white matters characterized by perivascular lymphocyte cuffing, neuronal loss, mild astrogliosis and microglial reaction that mainly affected the brainstem and cervical spinal cord. The perivascular infiltration consisted mainly of lymphocytes with few plasma cells, histiocytes and occasional macrophages. The leptomeninges of the frontal cortex showed mild thickening and lymphocytic infiltration. In the temporal cortex, there was a cortical focal petechial hemorrhage nearby with an area of subcortical demyelination which was confirmed by myelin stainings. In both of the temporal lobes, perivascular cuffing of lymphocytes were prominent in the periventricular regions. The basal ganglia also showed perivenous lymphocytic infiltration. Sections of the medulla oblangata showed similar lymphocytic perivascular cuffing and meningeal infiltration which is more prominent than other parts of the brain and particularly located at the periventricular zone (Fig. 1A). Granular ependymitis and astrogliosis were also observed. Small and medium sized neurons seemed to be reduced in number and the large neurons appeared to be preserved in the ventml horns of the cervical spinal cord (Fig. 1B). There was a patchy scattering of lymphocytes in the subarachnoid space and around some of the small vessels penetrating the white and gray matter of the spinal cord.

extractions.value: clinical features such as rigidity, abnormal postures and painful muscle spasms similar to that of stiff-man syndrome; progressive fatal course; presence of pathologic neurological signs and histopathological findings compatible with encephalomyelitis; continuous motor unit activity in electromyography
extractions.quote: The clinical presentation of rigidity, abnormal posture, painful spasms in thle distal limbs, motor and sensory deficits, hyporeflexia, sphincter pathology, a progressive fatal course, continuous muscle fibre activity in EMG and the histopathological findings of encephalomyelitis are compatible with the diagnosis of PEWR in this patient [1, 5, 6, 12, 13]. Neuropathological findings of encephalomyelitis with perivascular lymphocyte cuffing, infiltration, neuronal loss and mild astrogliosis, mainly affecting the brainstem and spinal cord, were also compatible with that of other PEWR cases.

Routine laboratory tests were normal except increased ESR and liver enzymes. Serum calcium, ionized calcium and parathormone levels were within normal limits. Antibody screens for viruses including HIV were normal or negative except antibody positivity for HCV. Serological studies for Treponema pallidum, Borrelia burgdorferi, Toxoplasma gondii and fungi were negative. Detailed tests for autoimmunity including anti-DNA, antinuclear, anticardiolipin and antimitochondrial antibodies, and tumor markers revealed no abnormality. CSF examination revealed mild pleocytosis (44 white blood cells/mm3, 80% lymphocytes) and elevation in protein content of 65 mg/dl, normal IgG index and polyclonal IgG banding. Viral and bacteriological screens of CSF were negative. Nerve conduction studies were normal.

[...] Liver biopsy showed histopathological findings compatible with active chronic C viral hepatitis with mild chronicity. HCV-RNA was detected by RT-PCR in plasma but not in CSF sample. Three weeks later, the patient developed acute pancreatitis that resolved with supportive treatment in a month. After the pancreatitis attack, she progressively deteriorated and the painful muscle spasms and rigidity increased both in frequency and intensity. Diazepam and baclofen treatment gave slight relief. Repeated EEGs showed diffuse slowing of background activity. CSF examination revealed blurred fluid with marked lymphocytosis 187 white blood cells/mm3, 95% lymphocytes) and further increase in protein content (200 mg/dl). Repeated serological tests for virus and tumor markers revealed no abnormality and cervical MRI showed mild atrophy. The patient died of pneumonia and secondary septicemia on the fourth month of her admission.
